blocks.content: When a system runs out of capacity there are only two directions to go: make the machine it runs on bigger, or run it on more machines at once. Those two directions are vertical scaling and horizontal scaling, and almost every other scaling decision in system design is really a variation on choosing between them, or figuring out how to combine both at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030194-252102335.png
blocks.alt: Vertical scaling grows one machine bigger; horizontal scaling adds more machines running the same workload

blocks.content: 1. What Vertical Scaling Means

Vertical scaling, sometimes called scaling up, means increasing the resources of a single machine: more CPU cores, more memory, faster disks. The software itself usually does not need to change at all, since it is still just one instance running on one machine, only now that machine has more room to work with.

This is often the very first scaling move a team makes, precisely because it requires no architectural change. A database or application that is starting to struggle gets moved to a bigger instance size, and the problem is solved, at least for a while, without touching a single line of code.

Because vertical scaling is such a small operational change, it is also the right first move even for a team that expects to eventually need horizontal scaling. Buying time cheaply with a bigger machine while the harder architectural work of statelessness and partitioning gets planned properly is usually a better sequence than rushing into a distributed design under pressure.

The tooling around this has also gotten much better over time. Modern cloud platforms let a team resize an instance with a few clicks or a single command, which is a large part of why vertical scaling remains such an attractive first option even for teams that are otherwise fairly sophisticated about infrastructure.
2. What Horizontal Scaling Means

Horizontal scaling, scaling out, means adding more machines that each run a copy of the same workload, splitting the total load across all of them rather than asking one machine to handle more of it. Instead of one server getting bigger, there are simply more servers.

This is a bigger structural commitment than vertical scaling, because the moment there is more than one machine handling requests, something has to decide how work gets distributed across them, which is exactly the job a load balancer exists to do, and the application itself has to be able to run correctly as multiple simultaneous copies rather than assuming it is the only one.

It is worth being precise that horizontal scaling means more machines doing the same kind of work, as opposed to splitting different responsibilities across different machines, which is a separate idea usually discussed under service decomposition or microservices. Both add more machines to a system, but they solve different problems.

A load balancer distributing requests across a horizontally scaled fleet needs its own strategy too, whether round robin, least connections, or something aware of each instance current load, which is its own topic but is worth remembering as the piece that makes horizontal scaling actually function from the outside.
3. The Ceiling On Vertical Scaling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030019-883146330.png
blocks.alt: Vertical scaling runs into rising cost per unit of capacity and, eventually, a hard limit on how big a single machine can get

blocks.content: Vertical scaling has a ceiling in two separate senses. The practical one is economic: the cost of hardware does not scale linearly, a machine with twice the CPU and memory of another typically costs meaningfully more than twice as much, so the cost per unit of capacity gets worse the bigger the machine gets. The harder one is physical: there is a largest machine size available at any point in time, and once a workload needs more than that, vertical scaling has genuinely run out of road, not just gotten expensive.

Horizontal scaling does not have this same ceiling, at least not in the same way. Adding a hundred and first server is not fundamentally different from adding the second one, which is why systems that need to grow far beyond what any single machine can offer eventually have no real choice but to scale horizontally.

It is worth noting this ceiling keeps moving outward as hardware improves, so a limit that felt hard a decade ago may not exist today, but the underlying shape of the argument, that there is always some largest available machine at any point in time, remains true regardless of where exactly that line currently sits.
3.1 Diminishing Returns Within A Single Machine
blocks.text: 3.1 Diminishing Returns Within A Single Machine

blocks.content: Even before hitting the hard ceiling of the largest available machine, vertical scaling frequently runs into diminishing returns well before that point. Doubling the number of CPU cores does not double the effective throughput of every workload, because many programs have parts that cannot run in parallel at all, and shared resources inside the machine, like memory bandwidth or lock contention, start to become the limiting factor before every core is genuinely being used.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285477367-595907170.png
blocks.alt: Whether doubling cores actually doubles throughput depends heavily on how parallelizable the workload is and how much contention exists on shared resources inside the machine

blocks.title: This is the same idea behind Amdahl law
blocks.content: The speedup available from adding more parallel resources is capped by whatever portion of the work cannot be parallelized at all. A workload that is ten percent inherently sequential can never run more than ten times faster, no matter how many cores are thrown at it.

This is a useful reality check before assuming a bigger machine automatically solves a performance problem. If the actual bottleneck is a single-threaded piece of code or lock contention between threads, doubling the core count can deliver almost no improvement at all, and the money would have been better spent finding and fixing that bottleneck directly.
4. Why Horizontal Scaling Needs Different Software
blocks.text: 4. Why Horizontal Scaling Needs Different Software

blocks.content: Vertical scaling is close to free from a software design perspective. Horizontal scaling is not. The moment a workload runs as many simultaneous copies, anything that assumed there was only one copy running becomes a bug: in-memory state that only one instance knows about, a background job that should only run once but now runs once per instance, a local file written by one request and expected to be read by the next.

This is really the deeper reason stateless design matters so much in modern system architecture. A stateless service, one that keeps no important data in its own memory or local disk between requests, can be horizontally scaled by simply running more copies of it behind a load balancer with no coordination problem at all. A stateful service needs a real strategy, covered in full in the stateful versus stateless architecture topic, before it can be horizontally scaled safely.

This is also why lifting an old, single-instance-assuming application straight onto a horizontally scaled fleet without any changes is a common source of subtle production bugs. The application runs, traffic is spread across instances, and everything seems fine until the first request that depends on state written by a different instance, at which point it fails in a way that never showed up in single-instance testing.

None of this means horizontal scaling is inherently more fragile, only that it trades a different, more visible kind of complexity for the scalability it buys. A well-designed stateless service handles this cleanly by construction, which is exactly why so much modern architecture advice centers on pushing state out of application servers and into purpose-built stores instead.
5. Cost Curves Compared

Say a workload currently needs roughly the equivalent of four standard-sized servers worth of capacity. Buying one machine four times the standard size, if it exists at all, commonly costs noticeably more than four times a standard machine, because larger instance sizes carry a price premium that grows faster than the resources themselves. Running four standard-sized machines behind a load balancer instead can often come out cheaper in raw hardware cost, at the price of the coordination complexity discussed above.

This crossover point, where horizontal scaling becomes cheaper as well as more scalable, is exactly why large systems tend to converge on horizontal scaling as their default posture over time, even when a single powerful machine could technically still handle current load.

These crossover numbers shift constantly as hardware pricing changes, so the right habit is recalculating them against current pricing when a real scaling decision is on the table, rather than trusting a rule of thumb that may have been true a few years ago but no longer reflects current instance pricing.

Raw hardware or instance cost is also not the only line item worth comparing. Operating a horizontally scaled fleet usually means more monitoring surface area, more deployment coordination, and more engineering time spent on the distributed-systems concerns covered throughout this topic, all of which are real costs that a simple sticker-price comparison leaves out.
6. Downtime During Scaling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030197-900609461.png
blocks.alt: Resizing a single machine vertically commonly needs a stop-and-resume cutover window; adding a new horizontal instance usually does not

blocks.content: Growing a single machine vertically frequently means stopping it, resizing it, and starting it again, or migrating its workload to a new, bigger machine, either way usually involving a cutover window where the service is briefly degraded or unavailable. Some modern cloud infrastructure supports resizing with a brief restart rather than a full migration, but a moment of disruption is still the common case.

Horizontal scaling avoids this almost entirely. Adding a new instance behind a load balancer means the existing instances keep serving traffic completely undisturbed while the new one spins up and joins the pool, which is a meaningful operational advantage on top of the raw capacity and cost benefits already covered.

This difference alone is often reason enough for a team serving traffic around the clock to prefer horizontal scaling for anything customer-facing, independent of the raw cost or ceiling arguments, simply because a maintenance window that customers never notice is worth quite a lot on its own.

Some databases and platforms now support online resizing that avoids a full restart, narrowing this gap, but it is still worth verifying explicitly for a specific database and cloud provider rather than assuming a seamless resize is universally available.
7. Where Vertical Still Wins

Vertical scaling remains the simpler, and sometimes the only practical, option for genuinely stateful systems that are hard to split, like a single primary database handling writes. Splitting write traffic across multiple independent machines requires partitioning or sharding the data itself, a significant undertaking covered elsewhere, so scaling the primary vertically is usually the first several steps taken long before that undertaking is worth it.

Vertical scaling is also simply less operationally complex. There is no load balancer to configure, no distributed state to reason about, and no question of which instance handled a given request. For a workload that a single sufficiently large machine can comfortably serve, reaching for horizontal scaling anyway adds real complexity for no corresponding benefit.

Simplicity also has a real operational value that is easy to underrate: fewer moving parts means fewer things that can independently fail, and a single well-monitored machine is genuinely easier to reason about during an incident than a fleet of a hundred, even if the fleet is individually more resilient to any one machine failing.
7.1 A Cost Detail People Forget: Licensing
blocks.text: 7.1 A Cost Detail People Forget: Licensing

blocks.content: Some enterprise software, particularly certain commercial databases, is licensed per CPU core rather than per machine, which flips the usual cost math in an easy-to-miss way. Running one large machine with sixteen cores can cost less in licensing than running four smaller machines with sixteen cores combined, purely because the licensing model charges per core regardless of how those cores are distributed across machines.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285481671-264365146.png
blocks.alt: Per-core licensing can make a single larger machine cheaper overall than several smaller ones with the same total core count

blocks.title: Worth checking before assuming horizontal is always cheaper
blocks.content: This is exactly the kind of detail that flips a decision that looks obvious from hardware cost alone. Anything running licensed commercial software is worth a specific licensing cost check before committing to a horizontal scaling plan.

Cloud providers increasingly offer usage-based or vCPU-based licensing for the same software specifically to soften this effect, so this is worth checking against current vendor pricing rather than assuming the traditional per-core model is the only option available.
8. Where Horizontal Scaling Wins

Stateless web and application tiers are the clearest case for horizontal scaling, since adding more identical, interchangeable instances behind a load balancer is close to the ideal scenario horizontal scaling was designed for. Traffic can grow far beyond what any single machine could serve, and capacity can be added or removed on demand as load rises and falls throughout the day.

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web-service
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web-service
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

codes.yaml:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web-service
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web-service

  maxReplicas: 30

    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

blocks.content: That configuration is a horizontal pod autoscaler, an increasingly common real-world example of horizontal scaling automated entirely: the platform watches a metric like CPU utilization and adds or removes instances on its own, within configured bounds, with no manual resizing decision needed at all.
8.1 How Automatic Horizontal Scaling Decides

The autoscaler configuration shown above works on a simple feedback loop: watch a metric, compare it to a threshold, and add or remove instances accordingly, always staying within a configured minimum and maximum.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285483537-650602779.png
blocks.alt: An autoscaler continuously compares a load metric against a threshold and adjusts instance count up or down within configured bounds

blocks.content: The metric chosen matters a great deal. CPU utilization is the simplest and most common choice, but for some workloads a more direct signal, like the length of a request queue or a custom application metric, predicts overload far earlier and more reliably than CPU alone, since CPU can look perfectly healthy right up until the moment a downstream dependency gets slow and requests start piling up.
8.2 Scaling Down Carefully

Adding instances under load is the easy half of autoscaling. Removing them safely is the half that causes real incidents when done carelessly, since an instance being terminated may still be mid-request, and simply killing it drops whatever it was doing. A safe scale-down waits for in-flight requests to finish and stops sending it new ones first, a pattern usually called a graceful drain, before the instance is actually removed.

blocks.title: Why this matters more than it sounds
blocks.content: Scaling down aggressively with no drain step is a common, entirely self-inflicted source of intermittent errors that only appear during exactly the low-traffic periods when a system is scaling down, which makes them confusing to reproduce and easy to misdiagnose as something else entirely.

The same graceful drain idea applies just as much to vertical resizing during a planned migration to a bigger machine: draining traffic away from the old instance before cutting it over avoids dropping in-flight requests, rather than assuming the migration tooling handles this automatically.
9. Hybrid Approaches
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285486107-545705966.png
blocks.alt: A common hybrid pattern scales the primary database vertically while scaling read capacity horizontally through replicas

blocks.content: Most large real systems use both at once rather than picking one exclusively. A common pattern is a primary database scaled vertically as far as it reasonably can be, paired with read replicas that scale read capacity horizontally, covered in depth in the read replicas topic. The write path, harder to split, gets the simpler vertical treatment; the read path, easier to duplicate, gets scaled out.

The stateless application tier in front of that database is almost always scaled horizontally on its own, completely independent of however the database underneath it is being scaled, which is a good illustration of why this decision is made per component, not once for the whole system.

Container orchestration platforms make this hybrid pattern easy to express directly in configuration: a stateful database workload pinned to a small number of larger nodes, and a stateless application workload spread thinly across many smaller nodes with autoscaling enabled, both managed by the same underlying platform but scaled by completely different rules.

Caching sits comfortably alongside this hybrid pattern too: a cache layer in front of the vertically scaled primary, itself scaled horizontally across a cluster, absorbs read traffic before it ever reaches the database, reducing how hard the primary has to be scaled vertically in the first place.

Recognizing this hybrid pattern by name is often the difference between a design that looks thoughtfully layered and one that reads as having applied a single scaling philosophy uniformly without considering that different parts of a system have genuinely different constraints.
10. Common Anti-Patterns

["Reaching for horizontal scaling and its added complexity before confirming a bigger single machine would not have solved the problem more simply.","Scaling a stateful service horizontally without first solving how its state gets shared, partitioned, or synchronized across instances.","Repeatedly resizing vertically as a reflex without ever noticing the workload has grown past what any single machine can offer.","Configuring horizontal autoscaling with no minimum instance count, causing a slow-starting cold instance to be the only thing handling a sudden traffic spike."]
items: Reaching for horizontal scaling and its added complexity before confirming a bigger single machine would not have solved the problem more simply.
Scaling a stateful service horizontally without first solving how its state gets shared, partitioned, or synchronized across instances.
Repeatedly resizing vertically as a reflex without ever noticing the workload has grown past what any single machine can offer.
Configuring horizontal autoscaling with no minimum instance count, causing a slow-starting cold instance to be the only thing handling a sudden traffic spike.

["Is the component stateless, or can its state realistically be made external and shared.","Has a concrete, measured limit actually been hit, not just an assumption that scaling will eventually be needed.","Does the workload run on software licensed per core, which can change the cost math significantly.","Would the operational complexity of load balancing and multi-instance coordination be worth it yet at current scale."]
items: Is the component stateless, or can its state realistically be made external and shared.
Has a concrete, measured limit actually been hit, not just an assumption that scaling will eventually be needed.
Does the workload run on software licensed per core, which can change the cost math significantly.
Would the operational complexity of load balancing and multi-instance coordination be worth it yet at current scale.

blocks.content: Running through this checklist explicitly, in writing, before a scaling decision is made turns what is often a reactive, under-pressure choice into a documented decision that the next engineer working on the system can understand and revisit later.
11. Real-World Examples

{"headers":["System","Scaling approach"],"rows":[["Stateless web or API tier","Scaled horizontally behind a load balancer, often with automatic scaling based on load"],["Primary relational database","Scaled vertically first, moving to partitioning or sharding only once vertical limits are reached"],["Read-heavy database workloads","Scaled horizontally through read replicas while the primary remains a single vertically scaled machine"],["In-memory caches","Scaled horizontally through a cluster with data distributed across nodes by consistent hashing"]]}

These examples are also a good illustration that the decision is rarely all-or-nothing even within a single system category. Two companies running what looks like the same kind of database workload can land on different points along this spectrum depending on their specific traffic shape, team size, and operational maturity.
11.1 Common Scale Triggers

Deciding when to scale, in either direction, needs a concrete trigger rather than a vague sense that things feel slow. A few signals show up repeatedly across real systems as the actual thing being watched.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285487789-495092431.png
blocks.alt: Several different signals, CPU, queue depth, or latency against an SLA, can each independently trigger a scaling decision

blocks.content: Whichever signal is chosen, it is worth setting the threshold with some margin below the point where users would actually feel pain, since scaling itself is not instantaneous. New instances take time to start, warm up, and start receiving traffic, so the trigger needs to fire early enough that added capacity arrives before the existing capacity is genuinely overwhelmed.
12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: This comes up in essentially every system design interview because it is the very first scaling decision any system faces. A strong answer treats it as a genuine trade rather than assuming horizontal scaling is always the sophisticated, correct answer: naming a component that is easier to scale vertically, like a primary database, alongside one that clearly benefits from horizontal scaling, like a stateless API tier, shows real judgment rather than a memorized preference.

It is also worth being ready to explain why horizontal scaling requires more than just adding machines: statelessness, load balancing, and often data partitioning all have to be addressed together, and glossing over that complexity is a common tell that the trade is not fully understood.
Vertical scaling asks one machine to do more. Horizontal scaling asks more machines to each do a little, and asks your software to be built in a way that makes that possible.

Bringing up the licensing and diminishing-returns nuances covered earlier in this topic, when relevant to the specific system being discussed, is a reliable way to stand out from an answer that only recites the textbook definition of each term.
12.1 A Common Follow-Up Question

A frequent follow-up asks how you would decide, for a brand new component, which direction to scale first. A grounded answer starts by asking whether the component holds state that is hard to split, like a primary database, in which case vertical scaling buys time cheaply while a longer-term partitioning strategy gets designed, versus a stateless component with no such constraint, which can usually go straight to horizontal scaling from day one.

blocks.title: The interviewer is really testing sequencing, not just knowledge
blocks.content: Naming that a team would start vertical for simplicity and only move to horizontal once a concrete, measured limit is hit reads as more mature than jumping straight to a fully horizontally scaled design for a system that does not need it yet.

A second common follow-up asks what signals would tell you vertical scaling has stopped being sufficient. The concrete answer is hitting the largest available instance size while still seeing sustained saturation, or seeing the cost curve cross over what an equivalent horizontal setup would cost, either of which is a specific, defensible trigger rather than a vague sense that it might be time to change approach.

Neither direction is inherently the more advanced or more correct choice. The right answer is always specific to the component in question, its state, its current measured limits, and what it would actually cost, in both money and complexity, to scale it the other way.
Key Takeaways

["Vertical scaling grows a single machine; horizontal scaling adds more machines running the same workload.","Vertical scaling is simpler but has a real ceiling, both economic and physical.","Horizontal scaling avoids that ceiling but requires software designed to run as multiple simultaneous copies, usually meaning statelessness.","Vertical scaling commonly needs a cutover window; horizontal scaling usually does not disrupt existing traffic.","Real systems typically combine both, choosing per component rather than picking one approach for the entire system."]
items: Vertical scaling grows a single machine; horizontal scaling adds more machines running the same workload.
Vertical scaling is simpler but has a real ceiling, both economic and physical.
Horizontal scaling avoids that ceiling but requires software designed to run as multiple simultaneous copies, usually meaning statelessness.
Vertical scaling commonly needs a cutover window; horizontal scaling usually does not disrupt existing traffic.
Real systems typically combine both, choosing per component rather than picking one approach for the entire system.
